stories.title: Trash Trouble: Did Singapore Waste End Up in Johor?
stories.headline_kid: Piles of construction rubbish were found dumped illegally in Johor, and Singapore is now checking if any of it came from here.
summary: Officials found a big pile of illegal construction waste dumped near a village in Pontian, Johor, Malaysia. Construction waste is stuff like broken concrete, bricks and rubble left over when buildings are built or torn down — a bit like the leftover scraps when you knock down a big block tower.

Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) said this waste is NOT allowed to be sent to another country for dumping. NEA is now working together with Malaysian officials to find out exactly what happened and where the waste really came from.

So far, NEA says it is 'not yet established' whether any Singapore companies were involved. This means investigators are still gathering clues, like detectives trying to solve a case, before they can point fingers at anyone.

Dumping waste illegally can hurt nature — it can pollute rivers, soil and even affect animals living nearby. That's why countries have strict rules about where construction waste must go, and why breaking these rules is taken very seriously.

lenses.me: If you've seen a construction site near your home, this story shows why the leftover rubble must be thrown away the proper way, not dumped secretly somewhere else.
lenses.family: Your family might think twice about hiring only trustworthy companies for home renovations, since illegal dumping can happen if firms try to save money the wrong way.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates can talk about why looking after the environment isn't just a Singapore job — it matters across borders too.
lenses.nation: This case affects how Singapore and Malaysia trust and work with each other on environmental matters.
lenses.world: It shows that waste and pollution don't stop at national borders — countries must cooperate to solve environmental problems together.

stories.title: The World Races to Build More Nuclear Power
stories.headline_kid: Countries everywhere are rushing to build more nuclear power plants because the world needs a LOT more electricity, fast.
summary: Nuclear power is made by splitting tiny particles called atoms, which releases a huge burst of energy — like a very powerful, invisible engine that heats water to make electricity. It doesn't burn coal or oil, so it produces much less smoke and pollution than some other power plants.

Experts say the world will need twice as much uranium (the special metal used in nuclear plants) by 2040. This is because more people, more electric cars, and more computer data centres (which power things like AI chatbots) all need electricity.

Because of this, countries are reopening old uranium mines, building new plants, and even trying wild new ideas — like pulling uranium out of seawater, or building a machine nicknamed China's 'artificial sun' that tries to copy how the real sun makes energy, called fusion.

Singapore has also been studying whether nuclear power could work here one day, since our small island doesn't have much space for giant solar farms. This story is a peek into how the world plans to keep the lights on in the future.

lenses.me: Every time you switch on a fan or charge your tablet, electricity comes from somewhere — this story is about where tomorrow's power might come from.
lenses.family: How countries generate electricity can affect how much your family's power bills cost in the future.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might enjoy imagining what a mini 'artificial sun' looks like — it's real science, not science fiction!
lenses.nation: Singapore is exploring nuclear power as one option for clean energy since we have limited land for solar panels.
lenses.world: Countries are racing to find enough clean energy to power a growing, more digital world.

stories.title: Thai Schools Practise 'Run, Hide, Fight' to Stay Safe
stories.headline_kid: After a sad and scary event at a Thai school, schools across Thailand are now practising special safety drills to protect students.
summary: Two weeks ago, something very upsetting happened at a school in Nonthaburi, Thailand — a young student brought a weapon to school and hurt many classmates. It was a shocking event that made schools all over Thailand think hard about keeping students safe.

This week, schools across Thailand held safety drills called 'run, hide, fight'. This means students practise three simple steps: run away to safety if they can, hide quietly if they can't run, or as a very last resort, try to protect themselves. It's a bit like how you practise fire drills, but for a different kind of danger.

Students at schools like Surasak Montri in Bangkok took part, hiding under tables and learning what to do calmly, guided by police officers. The goal is to make sure everyone knows exactly what to do if something like this ever happens again.

Singapore schools also have their own safety plans and practise emergency procedures regularly, even though such events are extremely rare here. This story is a gentle reminder that schools everywhere work hard to keep students safe, and it's okay to ask a teacher or parent if you ever feel unsure or worried.

lenses.me: Even though this happened far away, it's a good reminder to always listen carefully during your own school's safety drills.
lenses.family: Parents everywhere want to know their children are safe at school — this story might spark a conversation with your family about school safety.
lenses.friends: You and your classmates could discuss what you already do during fire drills or safety briefings at your school.
lenses.nation: Singapore's Ministry of Education also has emergency plans in place, and schools regularly practise how to respond calmly to unexpected situations.
lenses.world: Sad events like this remind countries around the world to keep improving how they protect students in schools.

stories.title: China Lands a Rocket Booster Like a Pro!
stories.headline_kid: A Chinese space company just landed a rocket booster back on Earth safely — something only three companies in the whole world can do!
summary: A Chinese space company called LandSpace successfully landed the first stage (the bottom part) of its Zhuque-3 rocket after launching it into space. This is a huge achievement — the booster came back down and landed gently on legs, just like in movies about rockets!

This makes LandSpace only the third company ever to pull off this trick, joining famous names SpaceX and Blue Origin. Landing a rocket booster safely means it can be used again for another launch, instead of being thrown away.

Think of it like reusing a paper airplane instead of crumpling it up and folding a brand new one every single time. Reusable rockets save a lot of money and materials, which could make space travel much cheaper in the future.
Cheaper rockets could mean more satellites in space for things like better internet, weather forecasts, and GPS — all things that even small countries like Singapore rely on every day.

lenses.me: This story shows that big dreams, like becoming a scientist or engineer, can come true with lots of testing and hard work.
lenses.family: Your family might enjoy watching rocket launch videos together — it's a fun way to learn about space science.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could try building and launching your own paper or model rockets to see the science in action.
lenses.nation: Singapore's growing space and technology companies can learn from and even work with firms developing cheaper reusable rocket technology.
lenses.world: Reusable rockets could make it cheaper to send satellites into space, helping countries everywhere get better internet, weather data and navigation.

stories.title: A Rare Purple Watch Made With a Singapore Shop
stories.headline_kid: A famous Swiss watchmaker teamed up with a Singapore watch shop to create a special purple watch — and only 50 will ever exist!
summary: Parmigiani Fleurier, a Swiss watch brand known for very careful, detailed craftsmanship, has launched new watches for 2026. One of them, called the Tonda PF Automatic 36mm Soft Violet SHH Edition, was made together with Sincere Fine Watches, a well-known watch shop right here in Singapore.

Only 50 of these purple-dial watches will ever be made. This is called a 'limited edition' — meaning there are only a small, fixed number of them, which makes each one rare and special, a bit like a rare trading card that not everyone can own.

The brand also released two other fancy watches to celebrate anniversaries. One of them, the Tonda PF Chronographe Mysterieux, has a clever design where parts of the watch face seem to disappear and reappear, showing off very advanced watchmaking skills.
This collaboration shows that Singapore isn't just a place where people buy luxury goods — local shops here work closely with world-famous brands to help create special products found nowhere else.

lenses.me: This story shows that even something small like a watch takes many skilled hands and months of careful planning to design.
lenses.family: It might spark a chat with your family about special items, like watches, that are sometimes given as gifts for big occasions.
lenses.friends: You and your friends might enjoy talking about other 'limited edition' collectibles you know, like special toys or trading cards.
lenses.nation: This shows Singapore's growing reputation as a hub where big global brands like to partner with local businesses.
lenses.world: It's an example of how companies from different countries can work together to create something unique that reflects both cultures.
